title: Industry positioning hypothesis notebook
body:
Purpose: quick, divergent set of messaging hypotheses and competitive notes for five target verticals. This is intentionally rough — a notebook of angles we can A/B in landing pages, demo scripts, and SDR sequences. Do not treat as final copy.

Structure: for each vertical: 1) core business problem we solve, 2) primary buyer personas, 3) proposed one-line positioning, 4) defensive/competitive landmines, 5) tactical experiments to validate messaging and early metrics to watch.

1) Fintech (payments, lending, wealth platforms)
- Core problem: High-volume transactional text (KYC, fraud signals, customer chat) where latency + regulatory traceability equate to clear cost and risk. Teams need deterministic inference that fits into audit trails and predictable spend.
- Personas: Platform engineering lead, ML infra manager, Head of Product (risk/compliance), CTO for mid-stage startups.
- One-line positioning hypothesis: "Predictable, auditable LLM inference for financial workflows — low cost per decision, SLA-backed availability, and turnkey privacy controls."
- Competitive landmines: incumbent cloud providers promising model access + managed endpoints; vendors touting ‘bank-grade’ but requiring heavy custom integration. Also, fintech buyers will ask for certs (SOC2, PCI implications) and for deterministic outputs for compliance.
- Tactical experiments: landing page A/B (emphasize SLA + audit logs vs emphasize per-decision cost savings), 2 pilot offers: 30-day FRAUD chat pilot (sample 50k requests/day), and a KYC batch scoring test (compare latency and token cost). Track: pilot time-to-value, cost per decision, number of flagged regressions in outputs.

2) Healthcare (clinical summarization, prior auth, patient triage)
- Core problem: Sensitive PHI + high-risk correctness requirements. Buyers demand provenance, model lineage, and isolation (private deployment). Latency sometimes matters (triage) but accuracy/traceability matters more.
- Personas: Chief Medical Information Officer, Head of Clinical AI, Privacy/Security lead, Engineering manager (integrations).
- One-line positioning hypothesis: "Private, auditable LLM inference you can certify into clinical pipelines — controlled models, KMS integration, and traceable outputs for audits."
- Competitive landmines: specialized clinical AI vendors with curated medical models; hospital IT inertia and long procurement cycles. Also regulatory nuance: FDA guidance, HIPAA concerns.
- Tactical experiments: whitepaper + checklist (How to validate LLM outputs for clinical use), invite 3 hospital partners for an isolated VPC pilot (on-prem light), run evaluation on standard clinical prompts (MIMIC-style synthetic set) to measure hallucination rates. Track: time to security approval, percentage of outputs passing clinical validation, time to integrate with EHR HL7/FHIR flows.

3) Legal (contract analysis, discovery, compliance)
- Core problem: Legal teams need reliable extraction and deterministic rerank/rerun behavior for repeatable audits. Cost matters for large corp legal workloads.
- Personas: GC/Head of Ops, Legal Ops/Paralegals, Enterprise Search/Knowledge Manager, Security & Compliance.
- One-line positioning hypothesis: "Deterministic, versioned LLM inference that makes contract QA and e-discovery repeatable and defensible."
- Competitive landmines: niche legal AI tools with pre-built parsers and annotations; fear of non-deterministic outputs undermining evidentiary use.
- Tactical experiments: create a legal-focused evaluation harness (contract extraction precision/recall), offer a proof-of-concept to legal ops with model version pinning + output diffs. Messaging test: emphasize 'versioned outputs' vs 'best-effort accuracy'. Track: reduction in manual review hours, number of change requests on model results, legal signoff velocity.

4) Enterprise SaaS (customer success automation, knowledge base, search)
- Core problem: SaaS product teams want to add LLM features without operationalizing an inference stack. They care about developer ergonomics, low latency for interactive flows, and predictable unit economics as usage scales.
- Personas: Product manager (growth/eng), Platform/Backend engineering lead, Head of Customer Success (ops).
- One-line positioning hypothesis: "Plug-in LLM inference that scales predictably with your product — dev-friendly APIs, built-in caching, and cost controls for PLG growth."
- Competitive landmines: turnkey API-first LLM providers with simple onboarding; open-source runtime projects that are free but require infra investment.
- Tactical experiments: developer sandbox with a sample Next.js app using Redwood API and Quickstart; run a ‘scale-to-100k-users’ load test and publish metrics (latency percentiles, cost per 1k requests). Messaging split: 'developer velocity' vs 'cost predictability'. Track: signup-to-first-call time, SDK adoption in trials, retention of trial projects.

5) Gov / Defense (classification, summarization, sensitive-data handling)
- Core problem: Strict network and compliance requirements, air-gapped/on-prem preferences, long procurement cycles and high emphasis on control and explainability.
- Personas: Program manager, Security compliance officer, Chief Architect (on-prem infra), procurement officer.
- One-line positioning hypothesis: "Deployable inference for constrained environments — private control plane, HSM/KMS integration, and hardened observability for audit and FOIA readiness."
- Competitive landmines: specialized defense contractors and heavy compliance certifications; customers may prefer in-house builds for policy reasons.
- Tactical experiments: risk-focused sales playbook and a compliance pack (artifacts: architecture diagram, threat model, audit checklist). Pilot: small-scale on-prem trial with locked-down telemetry + offline update process. Track: procurement objections, time to security assessment sign-off, cost to run per node.

Cross-vertical notes (common themes and recommended platform features to highlight)
- Versioning + reproducibility: emphasize model pinning, output diffs, and rerunability. This is a recurring buying criterion across legal, fintech, healthcare.
- Cost predictability levers: highlight batching, caching, and quantization recommendations. Give concrete examples: "Batching reduced token cost by ~X% on high-QPS endpoints in baseline tests."
- Private deploy options: present the three modes clearly (hosted, dedicated, private) with short bulleted tradeoffs. Use simple checklist: data residency, control plane location, KMS/HSM needs.
- Observability: show sample dashboard screenshots (placeholder) and tie to developer stories: alert on regressions tied to eval prompt sets.
- SLA/enterprise terms: mid-market and up will require clear statements around uptime and incident response — include a short FAQ for procurement.

Open questions and next steps (experiments we can run this quarter)
- Build 3 short vertical landing pages and 3 SDR sequences (one for each persona in each vertical) and run on small paid channels + organic outreach to partners.
- Ship vertical evaluation kits (prompts + scoring harness) so prospects can measure improvement vs incumbent.
- Prepare two pilot templates: a 30-day hosted pilot (fast) and a 90-day private trial (security-heavy).
- Internal ask: engineering to bake simple model-diff export and a one-click private deployment guide for pilot partners.

Quick wins for content creators (copy snippets to steal)
- Fintech headline: "SLA-backed inference for financial decisions — low-latency, auditable, and compliant."
- Healthcare headline: "Clinical-grade LLM inference with private deployments and audit lineage."
- Legal headline: "Make contract QA defensible: versioned LLM outputs for repeatable reviews."
- Enterprise SaaS headline: "Ship LLM features faster — predictable cost and developer-first APIs."
- Gov headline: "Hardened inference for sensitive environments: deploy where you need it, control what you log."

Notes to self: keep language concrete, minimize generic 'AI' fluff — buyers care about SLOs, cost math, integration effort, and evidence (benchmarks/pilot results). Next revision: replace placeholders with actual pilot numbers after talking to infra/solutions teams.
